{{Use dmy dates|date=October 2019}}
'''Walter Warner''' (1563&ndash;1643) was an English [[mathematician]] and [[scientist]].

==Life==
He was born in [[Leicestershire]] and educated at [[Merton College, Oxford]], graduating B.A. in 1578.<ref name = Pyle>[[Andrew Pyle (philosopher)|Andrew Pyle]] (editor), ''Dictionary of Seventeenth Century British Philosophers'' (2000), article Warner, pp. 858&ndash;862.[https://prinsjlm.wixsite.com/animated-mechanism  See also Jan Prins: Walter Warner (ca. 1557-1643) and his notes on Animal Organisms. Dissertation, Utrecht University, 1992]</ref>

At the end of the sixteenth century he belonged to the circle round [[Henry Percy, 9th Earl of Northumberland]], the 'Wizard Earl'. The  Earl's ‘three magi’ were Warner, [[Thomas Harriot]] and [[Robert Hues]].<ref>Stephen Coote, ''A Play of Passion: The Life of Sir Walter Raleigh'' (1993), p. 325.</ref> Percy paid Warner a retainer to help him with alchemical experiments (£20 per annum in 1595, rising to £40 in 1607).<ref>[[Steven Shapin]], A Social History of Truth: Civility and Science in Seventeenth-century England (1994), p. 366.</ref> He also belonged to the overlapping group around [[Sir Walter Raleigh]]. At this time he was mainly known for chemical and medical interests.<ref>Robert Lacey, ''Sir Walter Raleigh'' (1973), p. 320.</ref> It has been argued by Jean Jacquot that this group of experimental researchers, sponsored by Percy and Raleigh, represents the transitional moment from the still-magical theories of [[Giordano Bruno]] to real science.<ref>John S. Mebane, ''Renaissance Magic and the Return of the Golden Age: The Occult Tradition and Marlowe, Jonson, and Shakespeare'' (1992), p. 78.</ref>

He may have been associated with [[Christopher Marlowe]]'s study group on religion, branded [[atheist]]s, but confusion is possible here with [[William Warner (poet)|William Warner]].<ref>[[Christopher Hill (historian)|Christopher Hill]], ''Intellectual Origins of the English Revolution'', Revisited (1997), p. 129, indexed under William Warner.</ref>

After Henry Percy's death, he was supported by [[Algernon Percy, 10th Earl of Northumberland]], and then [[Sir Thomas Aylesbury, 1st Baronet|Sir Thomas Aylesbury]].<ref name = Pyle/> Warner edited Harriot's ''Artis Analyticae Praxis'' in 1631.<ref>{{cite EB1911 |wstitle=Algebra |volume=1 |page=619}}</ref> He met [[Thomas Hobbes]] through [[Sir Charles Cavendish]], who circulated Warner's works.<ref>George Henry Radcliffe Parkinson, Stuart Shanker (1999), ''Routledge History of Philosophy'' (1999), p. 222.</ref>

Warner was a friend of [[Robert Payne (clergyman)|Robert Payne]], chaplain to Cavendish;<ref>[[Aloysius Martinich]], ''Hobbes: A Biography'' (1999), p. 24.</ref> and this connection is frequently used to associate Warner with the [[Welbeck Academy]].<ref>{{cite book|author=Ted-Larry Pebworth|title=Literary circles and cultural communities in Renaissance England|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Ih1sRzuOAhMC&pg=PA94|access-date=3 April 2012|year=2000|publisher=University of Missouri Press|isbn=978-0-8262-1317-4|pages=94}}</ref> In 1634 Warner and Hobbes discussed [[refraction]].<ref>Stuart Clark, ''Vanities of the Eye: Vision in Early Modern European Culture'' (2007), p. 334.</ref> This acquaintance was later brought up against Hobbes in the [[Hobbes-Wallis controversy]].<ref>[[Steven Shapin]] and [[Simon Schaffer]] (1985), ''Leviathan and the Air-Pump'', p. 83.</ref>

With [[John Pell (mathematician)|John Pell]] he computed the first table of [[antilogarithm]]s in the 1630s.<ref>{{cite DNB|wstitle=Pell, John|volume=44}}</ref> [[John Aubrey]], relying on Pell's testimony, states that Warner had claimed to have anticipated [[William Harvey]]'s discovery of the [[circulation of the blood]], and that Harvey must have heard of it through a Mr Prothero. Pell also mentioned that Warner had been born without a left hand.<ref>[[Richard Barber]] (editor), ''John Aubrey, Brief Lives'' (1975), p. 320.</ref>

==Scientific work and legacy==
Warner was unpublished in his lifetime, but well known, in particular to [[Marin Mersenne]] who published some of his optical work in ''Universae geometriae'' (1646). He was an [[atomist]], and a believer in an [[Steady State theory|infinite universe]]. He was both a theoretical and practical chemist, and wrote psychological works based on Bruno and [[Lullism]]. Many manuscripts of his survive, and show eclectic interests; they include works related to the circulation of the blood.<ref name = Pyle/> Some of Warner's papers ended up in the Pell manuscripts collected by [[Richard Busby]];<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://archimedes.mpiwg-berlin.mpg.de/cgi-bin/archim/dict/hw?lemma=PELL&step=entry&id=d006 |title=Archived copy |access-date=7 February 2009 |archive-date=5 June 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110605100028/http://archimedes.mpiwg-berlin.mpg.de/cgi-bin/archim/dict/hw?lemma=PELL&step=entry&id=d006 |url-status=dead }}</ref> after his death the bulk of his papers were seized in 1644 by superstitious sequestrators.<ref>[[Keith Thomas (historian)|Keith Thomas]], ''Religion and the Decline of Magic'' (1973), p. 431.</ref> George John Gray, writing in the ''[[Dictionary of National Biography]]'', states that the table of 11-figure antilogarithms later published by [[James Dodson (mathematician)|James Dodson]] was believed to have passed to [[Herbert Thorndike]], and then to Busby; Pell's account in 1644 was that Warner had been bankrupt, and the creditors were likely to destroy the work.<ref>{{DNB Cite|wstitle=Dodson, James}}</ref>
